narrative:
The model estimated an 82% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is not a certainty, but it is a high-risk estimate, and it is why your law school application was denied: the admissions decision treated that risk as too great to admit you now. Your gender and race were not used.

The strongest reason was your third-year class decile. At 1, it was far from the accepted-student average of 5.79, and it pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar-exam failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. At 37, it was essentially at the accepted-student average of 37.18 and was the main factor pushing toward passing rather than failing. The third factor was your first-year class decile. At 2, compared with an accepted average of 6.00, it also pushed toward failure, though less strongly than your third-year standing.

To move forward, ask admissions whether human review or feedback is available. Focus on strengthening the academic record that most concerned the model: your third-year performance. Meet an academic advisor, take rigorous upper-level or analytical coursework if eligible, and build a record of sustained improvement. Consider retaking the LSAT only if practice tests show a meaningful gain. When you reapply, provide updated transcripts, a clear explanation of your improvement, and evidence of readiness for law school and bar study.
